question: Which of the following is the best way to elicit the "convergence- retraction nystagmus" of a patient with dorsal midbrain syndrome?

options.A: have the patient track an object which is being moved AWAY from him or her
options.B: have the patient track an object which is being moved TOWARD him or her
options.C: have the patient track an upward-rotating OKN drum
options.D: have the patient track a downward-rotating OKN drum

explanation: The classic signs of dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka "Parinaud syndrome") are: paralysis of upgaze defective (voluntary) convergence pupillary light-near dissociation convergence-retraction "nystagmus" eyelid retraction ("Collier's sign") The convergence-retraction "nystagmus" is not considered a true nystagmus but rather a disjunctive saccadic oscillation. To elicit this movement, the patient is asked to track a downward-rotating OKN drum which will elicit an attempted upward saccade. Instead of a normal upward saccade, the patient with this syndrome will exhibit convergence and retraction of both eyes since there is co-contraction of all horizontal extraocular muscles (the medial recti acting more forcefully than the lateral recti). However, voluntary convergence movements are minimal. Typically, upward saccades are initially affected but upward pursuit movements can become affected as well. Eventually, even vestibulo-ocular responses (i.e. Dolls' head responses) and Bell's phenomenon can be paralyzed. In children, the most common causes of dorsal midbrain syndrome are pinealoma and congenital aqueductal stenosis. In young adult women, it is typically caused by multiple sclerosis. In elderly patients, the most common cause is midbrain stroke.

question: An 11-year-old girl is referred to your clinic for a history of long-standing nystagmus. On examination, you note a right jerk nystagmus that worsens in right gaze, but improves on left gaze. Which of the following laws does this nystagmus obey?
explanation: "Alexander's law" states that the nystagmus is more pronounced when gaze is directed toward the side of the fast-beating component. In this case, there is a right jerk nystagmus, thus it worsens in right gaze and improves on left gaze. There is no such thing as "Listing's law" in Ophthalmology. However, there is something called "Listing's plane" which contains the center of rotation of the eye and includes its x and z axes (see "Motor Physiology" chapter in the Peds BCSC book). "Donder's law" states that every tertiary eye position is associated with a specific torsional rotation. "Sherrington's law of reciprocal innervation" states that contraction of a given muscle (e.g. medial rectus) is accompanied by a decrease in contraction of its antagonist (e.g. lateral rectus). This law is violated by Duane's syndrome where co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti can occur. "Hering's law of equal innervation" states that yoke muscles receive equal innervational input when they are activated. For example, when looking straight up, both superior rectus muscles receive the same magnitude of innervational input. This law is violated by the condition of dissociated vertical deviation (DVD). CORNEAL ABNORMALITIES.

question: You are examining a child who presents with corneal clouding of both eyes. Which of the following findings would most strongly rule-in a diagnosis of congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) versus congenital hereditary stromal dystrophy (CHSD)?
explanation: Both CHED and CHSD are potential causes of congenital corneal opacity. Since CHSD is extremely rare (e.g. only a few families have been reported in the literature), it is typically not remembered in the "S-T-U-M-P-E-D" mnemonic for different causes of congenital corneal opacity: Sclerocornea Trauma Ulcer Mucopolysaccharidoses Peters anomaly Endothelial (e.g. CHED) Dermoid Basically, the most salient difference between CHED and CHSD is that there is no edema in CHSD (and especially no epithelial edema), though the thickness may be slightly increased in CHSD compared to normal infants. CHSD is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by "flaky" opacities throughout the stroma. CHSD is painless and not associated with either tearing or photophobia. In CHSD and CHED, intraocular pressure and horizontal corneal diameters are normal. This helps to distinguish CHSD and CHED from congenital glaucoma. There used to be a CHED 1 and CHED 2 classification, but recent genetic studies have reclassified CHED type 1 as the same entity as Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPMD), as both are autosomal dominant on the same locus at pericentromeric chromosome 20. CHED type 2 is now reclassified as just CHED, and is autosomal recessive (BCSC Peds and Cornea 2017-2018).

question: What is the most common location of limbal dermoids?
explanation: A common associated syndrome of limbal dermoids is Goldenhar syndrome (aka "oculoauriculovertebral syndrome") whose other manifestations include hemifacial microsomia, ear deformities (including preauricular appendages), upper eyelid colobomas, and vertebral anomalies. A great way to remember this is that the inferotemporal limbus is closest to the ear lobe which itself is frequently involved in Goldenhar syndrome.

question: Which of the following is the major reason for long-term vision loss in infants with tears in Descemet's membrane caused by forceps injury?
explanation: Disruption of Descemet's membrane from forceps injury can result in stromal and epithelial corneal edema. However, this edema usually clears relatively quickly. This disruption can result in anisometropic astigmatism which commonly can cause long- term vision loss from amblyopia.

question: Which of the following features is MOST likely to be associated with megalocornea?

options.C: requires gonioscopy to be able to see the anterior chamber angle
options.D: carrier mothers have slightly enlarged corneal diameters

explanation: Megalocornea is a X-linked condition. Carrier mothers often have slightly enlarged corneal diameters. 90% of affected patients are male. The condition is usually not associated with increased intraocular pressure and must be differentiated from infantile glaucoma. Megalocornea is usually an isolated finding and is not progressive. It may be associated with lens subluxation, iris hypoplasia, radial iris transillumination defects, and ectopic pupil. Oftentimes, the anterior chamber angle can be seen directly without the need for gonioscopy. Comments: Mega = Large or size XL. The inheritance of megalocornea is X-Linked (XL). Therefore, MEGAlocornea = XL (a large sized cornea and X-Linked)

question: You are managing an 18-year-old patient with the ocular abnormalities shown in the photographs above. This patient is also taking a prostaglandin analog for glaucoma in both eyes. Mutations in which of the following genes is most likely to be responsible for this patient's ocular condition?
explanation: The photographs demonstrate the classic ocular findings of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome (ARS): (1) posterior embryotoxon; (2) iris strands; and (3) corectopia with possible hole formation. ARS is typically an autosomal dominant disorder with mutations in the PITX2 and FOXC1 genes demonstrated to cause this phenotype. (Image credit: Cogan Pathology Collection found at: http://cogancollection.nei.nih.gov). Comments: TIGR/MYOC = Juvenile OAG, OPTN = Normal Tension Glaucoma, OPA1 = Dominant Optic Atrophy Axe the Foxy (FOXC) Pix(pics) (PITX): Axe for Axenfeld, FOXC1 for first word, PITX2 for second word.

question: You are examining a 2-year-old child in the hospital who was admitted for jaundice. Your examination is notable for the anterior segment finding seen in the photograph above. The child's past medical history is also significant for pulmonary stenosis and developmental delay. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this infant?
explanation: The slit-lamp photograph shows posterior embryotoxon which is defined as a thickened, "prominent" Schwalbe line. It is seen in up to 15% of normal patients. I t is a characteristic finding in a variety of syndromes, most commonly Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. This child has jaundice, cardiac defects, and posterior embryotoxon which are characteristic findings of Alagille syndrome (AS). AS is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations of the JAG1 gene on chromosome 20p12. It typically involves the liver, heart, skeleton, and the eye. Other characteristic findings include a broaden forehead, pointed chin, butterfly hemivertebrae, and mild developmental delay. The corneal finding in Wilson's disease is a Kayser-Fleischer ring (not posterior embryotoxon). Comments: - Alagille is also known as Arteriohepatic dysplasia. In addition to posterior embryotoxon, it is also associated with myopia and a pigmentary retinopathy (there is a question about it in the Retina section).

question: What is the generally-accepted measurement cutoff that defines a newborn as having "microcornea"?

options.A: horizontal corneal diameter less than 7 mm
options.B: horizontal corneal diameter less than 9 mm
options.C: horizontal corneal diameter less than 10 mm
options.D: horizontal corneal diameter less than 11 mm

explanation: Microcornea (defined as corneal diameter less than 9 mm in the newborn and less than 10 mm at 2 years of age) can occur in a variety of other ocular conditions including PHPV, colobomas, and nanophthalmos. Microcornea is a condition characterized by a clear cornea of normal thickness, but whose horizontal diameter is less than 10 mm. Individuals with microcornea are typically hyperopic because their corneas are relatively flat. Because of this flat corneal curvature, these individuals are more prone to angle closure glaucoma. For those patients without angle closure glaucoma, still 20% (not 5%) of them will develop an open-angle glaucoma. GLAUCOMA.

question: Mutations in which of the following genes is most likely responsible for this child's condition?
explanation: This photograph depicts diffuse corneal edema as seen by the irregular corneal light reflex. In addition, you are told that the horizontal corneal diameters are 13.5 mm OU which are grossly abnormal (normal in newborn is 9.5-10.5 mm; normal in 1-year-old child is 10.0-11.5 mm). According to the BCSC, glaucoma should be suspected in any child whose corneal diameter is greater than 13.0 mm. Therefore, this child has congenital glaucoma until proven otherwise and should undergo an urgent examination under anesthesia with likely surgical intervention. Though primary congenital glaucoma typically occurs sporadically, it has been associated with gene mutations in certain families. The first gene demonstrated to be involved in congenital glaucoma was CYP1B1 which encodes a protein in the cytochrome P450 enzyme family. Other causative mutations involve the GLC3A, GLC3B and GLC3C genes. You should memorize some of the other glaucomas' gene associations: Axenfeld-Rieger: PITX2 or FOXC1 Juvenile-onset glaucoma: GLC1A (aka MYOC) Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma: LOXL1 Normal tension glaucoma: OPTN.

question: An 11-month-old child with a history of primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is brought in by his mother for a 2nd opinion regarding his management. His mother is frustrated because the child has already undergone one goniotomy by a prominent glaucoma specialist, but his intraocular pressure is still in the 30 mmHg range OU. Which of the following options is the next best step for this child?
explanation: Typically, most pediatric glaucoma specialists would attempt a second angle glaucoma surgery (e.g. another goniotomy or trabeculotomy) before moving on to trabeculectomy (+/- MMC) or a glaucoma drainage implant. The success rate of 1 or 2 angle surgeries for PCG in infants presenting from 3 months to 1 year is approximately 80%.

question: A 6-month-old child is referred to your clinic for chronic tearing and "wincing" OU that his mother has noticed since 1 month of age. His ocular exam is seen above. Which of the following ancillary tests is best at monitoring his response to treatment?
explanation: The photograph demonstrates the presence of corneal edema as can be seen by the irregular corneal light reflex. In a child, the primary diagnosis that should be ruled in/out is congenital glaucoma. The classic triad of symptoms for congenital glaucoma are bleparospasm, photophobia, and epiphora (i.e. tearing). This child deserves a full ophthalmic exam, most likely under anesthesia. Of the answer choices above, A-scan ultrasound is the most appropriate ancillary test to monitor disease progression. If one eye is growing excessively compared to the fellow eye, this may indicate poor IOP control in that eye. Remember, congenital glaucoma is primarily managed with surgery, not chronic medical treatment.

question: A 10-year-old child with a history of poorly-controlled juvenile open angle glaucoma presents to your office with intraocular pressures (IOPs) of 26 and 29 mmHg in the right and left eyes respectively. He has a history of Ahmed glaucoma drainage implants in both eyes. He is currently also taking daily methazolamide to help control his IOPs. Which of the following topical glaucoma medications would be LEAST effective given this patient's history?
explanation: This child is already taking a systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (CAI); therefore use of a topical CAI like brinzolamide (brand name: Azopt) would be ineffective. If topical glaucoma medications are indicated for a child (e.g. added control after multiple glaucoma surgical procedures), most specialists would choose the prostaglandin analogs given their lack of systemic side effects. As emphasized repeatedly on this website, the a2-adrenergic agonist, brimonidine (brand name: Alphagan), is contraindicated in children younger than 2 years old. In this age group, brimonidine can cause lethargy, hypotonia, and CNS depression. This medication should also be used with caution in older children. Comments: I don't disagree with the topical CAI while on a current oral CAI, but what about a tube shunt helping outflow and adding a prostaglandin analog to help with trabecular outflow? It seems that the tube will greatly diminish the effect of the latanoprost. And since the other 3 choices offered all work on aqueous production, this would seem to be most likely to help before the latanoprost. Latanoprost works in the uveoescleral outflow, not trabecular True, but the fact that there is a tube in place with high IOP says to me that no outflow is working well so wouldn’t aqueous suppression be more efficacious? Uveoscleral outflow is not IOP dependant, unlike conventional TM IRIS ABNORMALITIES.

question: An 8-year-old boy is referred to your office by his pediatrician for a baseline eye exam. Your slit-lamp exam is significant for the findings seen in the photo above. Which of the following statements is most likely true for this patient?

options.A: His underlying condition also features posterior subcapsular cataracts
options.B: This boy is at higher risk for pilocytic astrocytomas of the optic nerve
options.C: This ocular finding may be associated with spontaneous hyphemas
options.D: His underlying disease is caused by an autosomal recessive genetic disease

explanation: The slit-lamp photo shows multiple iris melanocytic hamartomas otherwise known as Lisch nodules. The presence of these nodules constitutes one of the criteria in the diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The clinical diagnosis of NF1 consists of the patient exhibiting 2 or more of the following criteria: a first-degree relative with NF1 6 or more cafe-au-lait spots 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma axillary/inguinal/or other intertriginous freckling 2 or more Lisch nodules a distinctive osseous lesion (e.g. sphenoid bone dysplasia) optic nerve glioma A "pilocytic astrocytoma" of the optic nerve is equivalent to an optic glioma. On neuro- imaging, optic gliomas often appear as "fusiform" or "sausage- shaped" or "kinked" enlargements of the optic nerve. Answer choice "A" refers to the presence of posterior subcapsular cataracts in neurofibromatosis type 2 (there are no characteristic lens changes in NF1). Answer choice "C" refers to what may occur in juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG). The iris lesions in JXG appear as vascularized yellowish or reddish nodules. Answer choice "D" is incorrect since NF1 is autosomal dominant in inheritance. According to U of Michigan's website on this, over 90% of NF1 patients will have Lisch nodules by the age of 6. NF-1 also associated with myelinated NFL and congenital iris ectropion. NF-2 also associated with cortical wedge cataract.

question: You are examining a patient with the peculiar iris abnormalities shown in the photo above. The patient also has twelve discrete hyperpigmented macules on his back and chest areas. What chromosome contains the genetic locus that is responsible for this patient's likely systemic syndrome?
explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts small, sharply-demarcated excrescences of the anterior iris surface known as Lisch nodules. This patient apparently also has multiple cafe-au- lait spots and thus can be clinically diagnosed as having neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1). As stressed repeatedly in board review books, mutations of a genetic locus on chromosome 17 are responsible for this phakomatoses. This fact can be conveniently remembered by the number of letters in the word "neurofibromatosis." Lisch nodules are hamartomatous growths that typically appear in NF-1 patients between ages 5 and 10 years. These nodules are rarely seen before the age of 3 years, while they are present in nearly 100% of all NF-1 adults. The clinical criteria for a diagnosis of NF-1 are summarized here (need 2 or more criteria): a first-degree relative with NF1 6 or more cafe-au-lait spots 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma axillary/inguinal/or other intertriginous freckling 2 or more Lisch nodules a distinctive osseous lesion (e.g. sphenoid bone dysplasia) optic nerve glioma Lastly, a summary of the other answer choices and their respective syndromes: chromosome 9 -- tuberous sclerosis (also chromosome 16) chromosome 22 -- NF-2 A suggested mnemonic (contributed by Dr. Matthew Weed) to remember the diagnostic critiera for NF-1 is: "CALBORN" (Cafe-au-lait spots, Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, Bony deformity, Optic glioma, Relative affected, Neurofibromas)

question: You are called by your local pediatrician to take a look at one of his patients. The pediatrician is concerned by some "iris abnormalities" that he has noticed. Your examination is significant for multiple hypopigmented areas of the iris of this child's left eye as seen in the photo above (arrow). Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this iris finding? (Please ignore this child's congenital heterochromia)

options.A: It can result in secondary glaucoma and corectopia
options.B: It is associated with optic gliomas and hyperpigmented macules of the skin
options.D: It can be associated with oculodermal melanocytosis

explanation: The photograph depicts multiple hypopigmented spots in the iris which are otherwise known as Brushfield spots. They are focal areas of stromal hyperplasia, surrounded by relative hypoplasia and are more common in patients with lightly pigmented irises. These spots are found in approximately 90% of individuals with Down syndrome (i.e. trisomy 21). The spots themselves have no consequence on visual function. Similar nodules, called Wofflin nodules can occur in normal individuals. Answer choice "A" refers to Cogan-Reese syndrome; choice "B" refers to Lisch nodules in association with neurofibromatosis type 1; and choice "D" refers to iris mammillations.

question: Which retinal lesion is associated with the facial skin abnormality depicted in the photo above?
explanation: The photo shows the typical appearance of adenoma sebaceum which is actually a misnomer since these facial lesions actually do not contain adenomatous or sebaceous structures on histopathological sections. A more modern term given to these facial lesions is a facial angiofibroma. Approximately 75% of patients with tuberous sclerosis have this facial lesion which first appears in childhood and may be mistaken for common acne vulgaris. Tuberous sclerosis (TS) is one of the phakomatoses. Other manifestations of TS include: retinal astrocytomas, "ash leaf spots," subungual and periungual fibromas, and seizures (80% of patients) from cortical tubers. The classic triad of TS, called Vogt triad, consists of seizures, intellectual disability, and facial angiofibromas. Comments Section: Tuberous Sclerosis: "Fits, zits, dimwits"

question: You see a 2-year-old with nystagmus from 3 months of age, poor vision in both eyes, and an incomplete barely visible iris in both eyes. His mother and 2 brothers all have this same finding. This patient is likely to have which of the following?
explanation: Aniridia is a disease marked by bilateral hypoplastic irides, foveal hypoplasia with poor visual acuity, and frequent nystagmus. Other associated common features include glaucoma, optic nerve hypoplasia, cataracts, and the development of diffuse corneal scarring later in life from limbal stem cell deficiency. The disease is caused by PAX6 gene mutations and can be hereditary or arise de novo. In those cases of hereditary aniridia there is no increased risk for Wilms tumor (also known as nephroblastoma) over the general population. In patients with seemingly sporadic aniridia, up to one third of patients will develop Wilms tumor and most are diagnosed with the tumor by 5 years of age. All children with sporadic aniridia should undergo genetic testing for the Wilms tumor genetic defect. Most patients with aniridia will have photosensitivity simply due to the large amount of light entering the eye. Myelinated nerve fiber layer is associated with refractive amblyopia but is not commonly associated with aniridia. Comments: Why is B incorrect? Aniridia can be part of the WAGR Syndrome , is inherited in an AD pattern and in this case mother and 2 siblings have the disease as well, which can suggest an AD inheritance pattern! Please explain me why B is wrong... I think this question should be corrected B is incorrect because it is much less likely than C. The question stem clearly points to aniridia. The vast majority of aniridia patients experience photosensitivity (C). Approx one third of aniridia cases are sporadic, and only one third of these are associated with Wilm's tumour. So about 1 in 9 patients with aniridia will have A or B, in contrast to the vast majority of patients who will have C.

question: A 10-year-old child is referred to you by her pediatrician for a "nystagmus workup." On exam, her visual acuity is 20/100 and 20/150 in the right and left eyes respectively. She indeed has horizontal jerk nystagmus. You are slightly confused by the child's exam since there does not appear to be much visible iris tissue. Both eyes have similar abnormalities. What corneal abnormality is most characteristically associated with this child's ocular condition?

options.A: apical thinning and acute episodes of eye pain

explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts the rudimentary iris stump that occurs in aniridia. The actual name of this disease is a misnomer since there is always some iris remnant present. The main ocular conditions that occur in aniridia are: chronic angle closure glaucoma progressive corneal opacification (due to limbal stem cell deficiency) nystagmus foveal hypoplasia cataracts (especially small anterior polar cataracts) The corneal opacification occurs due to limbal stem cell deficiency. Therefore, limbal stem cell transplantation is indicated if this opacification occurs (then followed by a corneal transplant). Alternatively, a keratoprosthesis can be considered for aniridic patients with significant corneal opacity. As stated ad nauseum elsewhere on this website, sporadic cases of aniridia are much more commonly associated with Wilms tumor. For these patients, a renal ultrasound is mandatory to exclude this life-threatening tumor.

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the abnormality seen in the photograph above?

options.A: If this is "typical", then this photograph is of a right eye; It may involve more posterior structures (e.g. retina)
options.B: If this is "typical", then this photograph is of a right eye; It is NOT usually associated with involvement of more posterior structures (e.g. retina)
options.C: If this is "typical", then this photograph is of a left eye; It may involve more posterior structures (e.g. retina)
options.D: If this is "typical", then this photograph is of a left eye; It is NOT usually

explanation: This photograph depicts an iris coloboma. This abnormality is due to failure of the embryonic fissure to close in the 5th week of gestation. There are two main classes of iris colobomas: "typical" and "atypical". Typical: located in inferonasal quadrant can be associated with colobomas of the ciliary body, choroid, retina, and optic nerve Atypical: located anywhere besides inferonasal quadrant not usually associated with colobomas of the ciliary body, choroid, retina, and optic nerve probably result from fibrovascular remnants of the anterior hyaloid system Therefore, if the iris coloboma shown above is "typical", then this photograph is of a right eye. CATARACT & LENS DISORDERS.

question: An 8-year-old child with Marfan's syndrome experiences significant ectopia lentis is his right eye with almost complete absence of zonular support. A trial of refractive correction is attempted, but this does not result in satisfactory vision. You plan on a lensectomy for this subluxed lens. Which of the following is likely the worst intraocular lens and/or visual rehabilitation option?
explanation: Though a somewhat-controversial topic, most pediatric ophthalmologists would leave the child aphakic. Relatively good visual acuity can be achieved with glasses and especially with contact lenses. Iris and scleral-fixated (e.g. glued or sutured) lenses are regularly placed in adult eyes. However, there is continuing debate on the safety of using these techniques in the eyes of children due to concerns of endothelial cell loss, de-enclavation, and suture breakage.1,2 Because of these uncertainties, most Ophthalmologists currently would leave the child aphakic after lensectomy and provide visual rehabilitation with glasses or contact lenses. Of the answer choices provided, a traditional anterior chamber intraocular lens would certainly be the worst choice for a child given the higher risks to the endothelium compared to either iris- or scleral-fixated methods. Comments: "de-enclavation" = loss of iris fixation. To enclavate the iris is to pierce or nail it with the lens, thus fixing it in place.

question: Which of the following is the best method of diagnosing Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) early in a child?
explanation: Although the "Kayser-Fleischer ring" is a characteristic finding in Wilson's disease, it typically is present late in the course of the disease and is therefore not a good method for detecting early disease. Instead, serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels should be obtained to definitively diagnose this serious disease early. Comments: I would say people put more stock into serum ceruloplasmin, Kayser fleischer ring, and urinary copper excretion. urinary copper excretion may be more important than serum copper. gold standard is the liver biopsy. Agreed. 24-hour urine copper excretion is more sensitive than serum copper and is always included in a diagnostic work-up.

question: A 4-year-old child presents acutely with a painful and red left eye. Her slit-lamp exam is significant for the corneal deposits seen in the photograph above. Her laboratory results are significant for a very elevated angiotensin- converting enzyme (ACE) level. Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this disease process in children as compared to adults?

options.A: the incidence of arthritis is much less frequent as compared to adults
options.B: the incidence of rash is much less frequent as compared to adults
options.C: the incidence of panuveitis is much more frequent as compared to adults
options.D: the incidence of lung involvement is much less frequent as compared to adults

explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts the classic "mutton-fat" keratic precipitates of a granulomatous uveitis. The abnormally elevated ACE level implies a diagnosis of sarcodosis which may present differently in children as compared to adults. In young children (<5 years old), lung involvement in sarcoidosis is much less frequent, but associated rash and arthritis are more frequent. As in adult ocular sarcoidosis, anterior uveitis is much more common than panuveitis. Lastly, one must keep in mind that the ACE level in normal children is typically higher compared to adults. Therefore, a borderline elevated ACE should not be used as the sole way to diagnose sarcoidosis in young children. Comments: Also, sarcoid-like disease presenting in kids must think of Blau Syndrome, where they have a typical rash at a very young age, and can test for NOD2/CARD15 mutation (which, interestingly, is near the Crohn's mutation)

question: His pediatrician note states that he is at the 2nd percentile of height and that he has "stubby fingers and toes." Besides dispensing glasses, which of the following is generally recommended for patients with this disorder?
explanation: This child presents with high myopia, brachydactyly, and relatively short stature. In addition, the clinical vignette implies that he also has microspherophakia. These constellation of clinical findings are consistent with Weill-Marchesani syndrome (WMS). There are no formal criteria for the diagnosis of WMS. Other abnormalities in this syndrome include ectopia lentis, joint stiffness, heart defects, and a broad head (brachycephaly). One way to remember WMS is that its phenotype is somewhat the opposite of Marfan's syndrome patients who are tall, have long limbs, and hyperflexible joints. The only mutations of one gene have been definitively proven to be associated with WMS. This gene is called ADAMTS10 which encodes a zinc-dependent protease. Mutations in another gene, FBN1 (encoding fibrillin-1), also have been implicated in one large family affected by WMS. The small, loose lenses of WMS patients may move anteriorly and result in pupillary block glaucoma with markedly-high IOPs. Therefore, it is generally recommended to perform prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomies to prevent this IOP spike. Cycloplegic use (answer "B") would be appropriate during the actual attack of pupillary block glaucoma since it would allow the small lens to move back posteriorly. Comments: BCSC Notes: "prophylactic LPI or lensectomy may be indicated" but does not expand. Could you please explain the reasoning to perform one over the other? I think most would say to start with the more conservative option first (i.e. LPI). Lensectomy is very aggressive as an initial treatment. Is this the disease where two LPI's per eye, 180 degrees apart, are recommended due to the small shifting crystalline lens? Yep. You do 180^ apart LPIs for ectopic lentis (caused by trauma, PXE,Marfa, homocystinuria, WMS, Ehlors-Danlos, Sulfite oxidase deficiency(.

question: You are called to the nursery to examine a newborn child with a relatively-dense central nuclear cataract of the right eye. His ocular exam is otherwise normal in both eyes. His father is frantic because he had a similar condition as a child and did not receive timely intervention. What is the generally accepted timeframe for when cataract surgery should be performed for this child?

options.A: cataract surgery is not indicated at this time

explanation: You are told in the clinical vignette that the cataract is "relatively-dense" and "central." From these descriptions, this cataract is likely amblyogenic and should be removed in a timely fashion. According to the BCSC, visually-significant unilateral congenital cataracts should be removed before 6 weeks of age while bilateral congenital cataracts should be removed before 10 weeks of age. Comments: Another user somewhere on this site came up with the following: Single = Six weeks Two = Ten weeks.

question: A 6-year-old child is referred to you by his pediatrician since she noticed an abnormal red reflex in both of the child's eyes. His slit-lamp exam is significant for the lens opacities OU seen in the photograph above. His mother states that the child complains of frequent tingling in the hands, feet, and the perioral area. Despite these symptoms, his mother states that the child is the smartest one in his class. Which of the following disorders is most likely the cause of this child's findings?
explanation: The slit-lamp photo shows the classic appearance of a "Christmas tree cataract" (i.e. "multicolor flecks"). The two conditions that this type of lens opacity can be associated with are: myotonic dystrophy and hypoparathyroidism. The symptoms of hypoparathyroidism are related to the low serum calcium levels that this condition induces. Therefore, these patients commonly experience paresthesias in their extremities and perioral region as well as the phenomenon of tetany. This latter sign can be elicted via tapping on the root of the facial nerve to induce tetany of the facial muscles (i.e. Chvostek's sign). These patients typically have normal intelligence. Patients with myotonic dystrophy can exhibit "myotonia" or inability to relax muscles when stimulated. The typical clinical vignette illustrating this is a patient who cannot release their handshake quickly. In contrast to patients with hypoparathyroidism, these patients typically display low intelligence. Other features of myotonic dystrophy (especially "classic" form) are ptosis, CPEO (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia), peripheral pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. The typical cataract associated with Lowe's syndrome is the "thin disciform" cataract. Patients with myotonic dystrophy type I (DMI) are known to have low intraocular pressures and it is hypothesized to be secondary to ciliary body detachments. Comments: For myotonic dystrophy -- imagine Frankenstein! He would have a hard time releasing a handshake, isnt too bright, cant see very far (xmas tree cataracts) definitely has ptosis, his eyes dont move around much (CPEO), and certainly has cardiac conduction issues from those bolts on his neck they electrocute him with.

question: What is the underlying cause for this child's systemic and ocular disorders?

options.B: Defect in latent transforming growth factor beta-binding protein 2 (LTBP2)
options.C: Sulfite oxidase deficiency or molybdenum cofactor deficiency

explanation: The photograph depicts a subluxed crystalline lens. There are several causes of luxated, or ectopic, lenses in children. The condition can be isolated, part of a multisystem disorder, or due to trauma and the most important conditions (according to the BCSC) are listed below: Associated with systemic conditions: Marfan syndrome Homocystinuria Weill-Marchesani syndrome Sulfite oxidase deficiency Isolated ocular conditions: Trauma Aniridia Iris coloboma Congenital glaucoma Hereditary ectopia lentis Ectopia lentis et pupillae Congenital megalocornea with zonular weakness In this case, in addition to ectopia lentis, this infant presents with recurrent seizures, hypertonia, and deep set eyes. These features are consistent with the very rare disease, sulfite oxidase deficiency. Sulfite oxidase oxidizes potentially toxic sulfites to nontoxic sulfates in the final step of the sulfur amino acid metabolism pathway. This enzyme requires molybdenum as a cofactor and the majority of cases are caused by deficient levels of this cofactor while a minority of cases are caused by deficiency of the enzyme itself. The prognosis is uniformly terrible with most children dying before the age of 5 years. WRONG ANSWERS (Choice A): Marfan syndrome is the syndrome most frequently associated with subluxated lens (presented in approximately 80% of patients). The lens is most often subluxated superiorly (think marFAN; superior on the ceiling): It is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in FBN1 gene which makes fibrillin-1 protein. Patients are tall with long limbs/fingers, flexible joints, cardiovascular abnormalities (leading cause of death in patients), scoliosis and chest deformities. Other ocular abnormalities include an increased axial length with high myopia and increased risk of retinal detachment. (Choice B): LTBP2 mutation causes primary megalocornea with zonular weakness which leads to secondary glaucoma from anterior lens displacement. The primary treatment is lens extraction. (Choice D): Mutations in ADAMTS10 gene has been linked with Weill- Marchesani syndrome. Patients are short, with short limbs and brachydactyly (can be thought of as the opposite in appearance of Marfan patients). Lenses are microspherophakic and can dislocate into the anterior chamber when lying supine. Prophylactic laser iridectomy or lens extraction may be indicated. The condition can be inherited in an autosomal recessive or dominant fashion. Comments: You can use the memory tool: WATCH HIM SEE W: Weill-Marchesani A: Aniridia T: Trauma C: Congenital glaucoma H: Hereditary ectopia lentis H: Homocystenuria and Hyperlysinemia I: Iris coloboma M: Marfans S: Sulfite oxidase defeciency and Syphillis E: Ehlers-Danlos E: Ectopia lentis et pupillae.

question: A 15-year-old teenager presents to your clinic with the slit-lamp finding as shown in the photograph. He has a personal caregiver because of his intellectual disability and also has a history of deep vein thrombosis. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment of this patient's systemic disorder?

options.A: blood pressure control to decrease rate of aortic dilation; possible elective aortic repair
options.D: dietary restriction of methionine and supplementation with folate,

explanation: This patient presents with ectopia lentis, intellectual disability, and a history of thrombotic events. These classic signs are likely the result of homocystinuria which is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a deficiency of cystathionine beta synthase. Other systemic abnormalities include a marfanoid habitus (i.e. tall, long limbs), pectus excavatum, and seizures. Other ocular abnormalities include myopia, glaucoma, and optic atrophy. There is no cure for homocystinuria, but its effects (especially on intellectual disability and thrombosis) can be greatly diminished if the affected individual is treated with high doses of vitamin B6 and follows a low methionine diet earlier in life.

question: A 1-month-old child with a history of galactosemia presents to your clinic for management of his bilateral cataracts. You perform lensectomies on both his eyes and decide to leave him aphakic OU. His current cycloplegic refraction is: +12.00 OU. You decide to prescribe him aphakic spectacles. Which of the following is the most appropriate power of these spectacles?

options.A: bifocal lens with distance power of +12.00 sphere OU; add power of +3.00 OU
options.B: bifocal lens with distance power of +10.00 sphere OU; add power of +3.00 OU
options.C: single vision glasses with power of +12.00 sphere OU
options.D: single vision glasses with power of +14.00 sphere OU

explanation: This child is only 1-month old and is unlikely to be able to use bifocal spectacles effectively. For these young infants, because their world is at their arms' length, the power for aphakic spectacles is chosen to correct for near vision, and hence they are given more add power than the cycloplegic refraction, to leave the infant slightly myopic. So in order for this child to have visual stimulus that is most appropriate for his viewing distance, which is 0.5 meters away, a overcorrection of hyperopia towards myopia of - 2D is utilized. Ignoring vertex distance, prescribing a +14.00 for this child with a +12.00 cycloplegic refraction will leave him with the desired two diopters of myopia. If one was putting an intraocular lens (IOL) into the eye, then the IOL calculation is aimed for hyperopia for the child's eye to grow and reach emmetropia. This means that the IOL power is less plus (for example, if the IOL master reports +26 D to reach a spherical equivalent of 0 D, then one would choose +24 D or +23 D for +2 D of hyperopia as the outcome). But we do not ever want to leave any child hyperopic who cannot accommodate -- that would cause refractive amblyopia. So if we put an IOL into the eye aimed for hyperopia, we would prescribe glasses with more add power to leave the child with slight myopia. (So yes, it is giving spectacles to cancel out the IOL power in anticipation for the eye to grow and the spectacle power to decrease over-time.) Aphakic spectacles are not a good choice in cases of monocular aphakia due to induced aniseikonia (i.e. image size disparity). For monocular cases, contact lenses are the preferred treatment modality. It is true that, in practice, even for bilateral aphakic patients, we prescribe contact lenses. But the concept of aniseikonia does not apply so we can get away with aphakic spectacles. UVEITIS.

question: What is the order of frequency of uveitis for the following childhood arthritis diseases (from most to least frequent)?
explanation: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common cause of uveitis in the pediatric age group. The main subgroups of JIA are: (1) oligoarthritis; (2) rheumatoid factor (RF)- negative polyarthritis; (3) psoriatic arthritis; (4) enthesitis-related arthritis; and (5) systemic arthritis (i.e. Still's disease). Of these, anterior uveitis (10-30% of cases) is most likely to occur in the oligoarthritis variety. This subgroup is defined by a persisting arthritis that lasts greater than 6 weeks and affects 4 or less joints during the first 6 months of the disease. RF is almost always absent in these patients. ANA is typically positive in both the oligo- and polyarthritis varieties. Anterior uveitis occurs in approximately 10% of patients in both the RF-negative polyarthritis and psoriatic arthritis subgroups. Uveitis rarely ever occurs in systemic arthritis (i.e. Still's disease).

question: A 10-year-old girl presents to your office with the corneal abnormality shown in the photo above. Though difficult to measure, you estimate her intraocular pressure to be 40 mmHg despite the use of maximally-tolerated medications including an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. She also has a history of joint pains affecting both knees and wrists. Which of the following would be the best choice in terms of intraocular pressure control?

options.A: increase in dosage of the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor

explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts band keratopathy with its characteristic calcium deposits at the level of the epithelial basement membrane and Bowman's layer. This young girl also has pain in 4 joints leading to a presumptive diagnosis of pauciarticular/oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic (rheumatoid) arthritis (JIA). Glaucoma is a frequent complication of JIA either from the process itself (e.g. smoldering inflammation recalcitrant to therapy), as a side effect of corticosteroid use, or as a consequence from multiple intraocular procedures (e.g. cataract surgery, vitrectomy). Though filtering surgery can be attempted (e.g. standard trabeculectomy, ExPress shunt), they are associated with a high risk of failure since the blebs scar over quickly. Though angle surgery may be effective in some of these children, the currently-preferred choice is insertion of a glaucoma drainage implant (e.g. Baerveldt, Ahmed, Molteno, etc). Lastly, it is highly recommended that the inflammation of JIA be as well controlled as possible before inserting a drainage implant since the risk of post-operative hypotony is very high in actively-inflammed eyes. Many specialists would also give a "stress-dose" of systemic corticosteroids/immunosuppressives prior to the surgery and during the immediate post-operative period to prevent hypotony. Comments: This is what the book says, but you had a previous question that said do a goniotomy and a repeat goniotomy before going to a tube. That question should probably be changed. That question was probably a typical juvenile or congenital glaucoma, in which angle surgery is the primary treatment. This is a bit different - think of it more as a uveitic glaucoma than juvenile. Ideally if someone's IOP were 40 wouldn't you put in an Ahmed? It would start working immediately rather than the Baerveldt which would take some time for the rip cord to be pulled etc. Additionally a valved glaucoma drainage implant such as an Ahmed would be preferred in a uveitic glaucoma patient (given the risk for hypotony) This is exactly what my glaucoma attending says Maybe it's different in children, but a valved GDI (like the Ahmed) is far and away the best choice for immediate IOP control in uveitics. I don't know anyone who would use a Baerveldt or Molteno in this case.

question: You are participating in the management of a 5-year-old child with a history of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The child is currently taking weekly oral doses of methotrexate which is alleviating his joint pain significantly. Which of the following is the most common adverse effect of methotrexate in children?
explanation: Methotrexate is oftentimes the first-line immunosuppressive that is used to treat both arthritis and uveitis in children since long-term systemic corticosteroids can have significant side effects in children (e.g. growth retardation, bone fractures, etc). The most common adverse effect of oral methotrexate is gastrointestinal disturbance (e.g. nausea/vomiting, diarrhea) which can be minimized by concurrent folic acid use or using intramusclar/subcutaneous injections instead). There are several serious (but fortunately rare) complications with methotrexate use including: hepatic toxicity, interstitial pneumonitis, and myelosuppression.

question: Which of the following is the most accurate diagnosis of this child's condition?
explanation: This child presents with a polyarthritis, skin rash, band keratopathy, anterior uveitis (granulomatous in this case), and multifocal choroiditis in an apparent autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. These characteristics are consistent with a diagnosis of Blau syndrome which is also called Jabs syndrome or familial juvenile systemic granulomatosis.1 This uncommon disorder is most often confused with juvenile idiopathic (rheumatoid) arthritis and sarcoidosis due to the findings of granulomatous anterior uveitis and band keratopathy. However unlike either of these disorders, Blau syndrome is a hereditary disease with the causative gene (NOD2) found on chromosome 16. Unlike sarcoidosis, there is no pulmonary involvement or adenopathy in this syndrome. In addition unlike Blau syndrome, JIA does not manifest with multifocal choroiditis and sometimes has positive ANA titers. Other ocular complications described with Blau syndrome include: ischemic optic neuropathy, cystoid macular edema, neovascularization resulting in vitreous hemorrhage, cataract, and glaucoma. Visual prognosis is guarded even with aggressive therapy with systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressives. As an aside, Heerfordt-Waldenstrom syndrome is a type of sarcoidosis syndrome characterized by uveitis, parotitis, fever, and facial nerve palsy. RETINA.

question: What two diseases have retinal findings most similar to retinopathy of prematurity?

options.A: Incontinentia pigmenti and Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)
options.B: Usher syndrome and Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)
options.C: Incontinenti pigmentia and Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV)
options.D: Usher syndrome and Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV)

explanation: Sometimes it seems that the weirder and more rare the disease, the more likely you are to encounter it on your test; Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) and FEVR are no exception to the rule. They both have retinal findings similar to retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) with some noteworthy exceptions that allow you to distinguish each from ROP. FEVR is a genetic eye disorder affecting the growth and development of blood vessels in the retina associated with vitreous traction leading to peripheral exudation, peripheral retinal breaks, and incomplete peripheral retinal vascularization. The fundus appearance can be very similar to ROP. FEVR is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, however, so examination of family members may be helpful. Keep in mind that there is variable expressivity so some patients with FEVR will have only mild retinal findings that are asymptomatic. Prematurity is also not a risk factor for FEVR; if a clinical vignette describes a normal sized infant from a normal pregnancy with fundus findings typical of ROP then you should be thinking about FEVR rather than ROP. IP, or Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome, is a X-linked dominant disease involving the eyes, skin, and brain. It is lethal in hemizygous males so if a clinical vignette describes a male with findings of ROP then you know that the answer choice is not IP. Skin findings include bullae on the extremities and hyperpigmented macules on the trunk. Brain abnormalities are common and include microcephaly, seizures, and intellectual disability. Finally the ocular findings are very similar to ROP and include incomplete peripheral vascularization leading to neovascular membranes leading to retinal detachment.

question: You are called to see a 3-day-old child for possible neonatal conjunctivitis of both eyes. During the course of your complete eye exam, you detect a mild amount of intraretinal hemorrhages OU on dilated fundus exam. The child otherwise appears healthy and attentive. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this child?

options.B: hematologic workup for possible coagulation disorder
options.C: imaging for other evidence of non-accidental trauma
options.D: report this incident immediately to child protective services

explanation: Retinal hemorrhages from the birth trauma of vaginal delivery is fairly common with newborns. These retinal hemorrhages rarely persist beyond the first month of life. In contrast, the retinal hemorrhages of non-accidental trauma (i.e. "shaken baby syndrome") are typically much more extensive and can be associated with evidence of retinal tissue disruption (e.g. perimacular folds, traumatic retinoschisis). Lastly, these children are almost always very ill with approximately 1/3 of them succumbing to their associated intracranial injuries.

question: Which of the following descriptions most accurately describes stage 3 retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?

options.D: ridge with or without small tufts of fibrovascular proliferation

explanation: The International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP) describes ROP by stage, zone, and extent. Worse forms of ROP are associated with higher stages and lower zones. The stages of ROP: Stage 0: immature vascularization (no ROP) Stage 1: demarcation line (i.e. has no height) Stage 2: ridge with or without small tufts of fibrovascular proliferation (i.e. has height) Stage 3: ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation Stage 4: subtotal retinal detachment (4A - extrafoveal RD; 4B - RD including fovea) Stage 5: total retinal detachment The "zones" or location of involvement of ROP: Zone I (i.e. posterior pole): circle (centered on the optic disc) with a radius of 30 degrees (i.e. approximately twice the disc-to-fovea distance) Zone II: from edge of zone I to point tangetial to nasal oral serrata and around to area near the temporal equator Zone III: residual cresent anterior to zone II The "extent" of disease is specified as hours of the clock as the examiner looks into the eye (e.g. "3 clock hours of involvement") "Plus disease" is added when vascular shunting is so severe that the posterior pole veins are enlarged and the arteries are tortuous. The Cryotherapy for Retinopathy of Prematurity (CRYO-ROP) defined "threshold disease" as 5 contiguous or 8 total clock-hours of stage 3 in zone I or II with plus disease. The Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) trial further classified ROP into either type 1 or type 2 disease. Laser treatment to the avascular retina is recommended for any eye with type 1 ROP: Type 1 ROP o Zone I, any stage with plus disease o Zone I, stage 3 without plus disease o Zone II, stage 2 or 3 with plus disease Type 2 ROP o Zone I, stage 1 or 2 without plus disease o Zone II, stage 3 without plus disease.

question: A patient is referred to you for the retinal lesion shown in the above photo. Which of the following systemic findings would most likely be found in association with this lesion?
explanation: The photograph depicts a redidsh-orange vascular tumor that is fed by a dilated, tortuous retinal artery and drained by an engorged vein. These features are classic for a retinal capillary hemangioblastoma. When these lesions are detected, a systemic evaluation is warranted to search for the myriad systemic findings that can occur with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). This syndrome is one of the classic phakomatoses (i.e. neuro-oculocutaneous syndromes) that are widely tested on Ophthalmology board exams. The retinal capillary hemangioblastoma is typically seen between the ages of 10 and 35 years. These vascular tumors can leak fluid into the macula with or without exudate retinal detachment. Also, these tumors can lead to vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment. These retinal tumors are typically treated with either photocoagulation or cryotherapy. Some key facts regarding VHL syndrome: Caused by mutation of a gene (VHL - a tumor suppressor gene) on chromosome 3p26. Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern; high penetrance (varies by mutation) and variable expression. Central nervous system tumors can include: 20% of VHL patients have hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum, medulla, pons, and spinal cord. Other findings include: renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytomas, cysts of the kidney/pancreas/liver, cardiac rhabdomyomas. The primary cause of death from this condition is from either cerebellar hemangioblastomas or renal cell carcinoma. WRONG CHOICES: The distractor answer choices are listing some classic findings in other phakomatoses. Acoustic neuromas are classically found in neurofibromatosis type 2. Meningeal angiomas (causing seizures) are more likely found in Sturge-Weber syndrome. Intracranial (especially midbrain) arteriovenous malformations are seen in Wyburn-Mason syndrome.

question: A 17-year-old Air Force recruit is referred to you after failing his vision test requirement to become a fighter pilot. His best corrected visual acuity is 20/40 and 20/70 in the right and left eyes respectively. His dilated fundus exam is seen above. Which of the following is a characteristic of this patient's likely condition?

options.A: color deficiency but without progressive loss of visual acuity
options.B: progressive loss of color vision and "hemeralopia"

explanation: The fundus photo shows a Bull's eye maculopathy and loss of the foveal reflex OS>OD (i.e. "polymorphic sheen" or "beaten-bronze" appearance). In addition, there are surrounding yellow deposits ("pisciform flecks") in the paramacular area and relative sparing of the peripapillary retina. These features are consistent with a diagnosis of Stargardt disease. Since the flecks appear to be diffusely distributed throughout the posterior pole, you can say that this patient has fundus flavimaculatus (FF). The hallmark FA finding of Stargardt's/FF is the "dark choroid" sign whereby the retinal vessels are highlighted against a hypofluorescent choroid in the early phases of the FA. This is thought to be due to blockage from diffusely distributed lipofuscin. Stargardt's/FF is the most common juvenile macular dystrophy with age of onset typically in the early teenage years. The end visual acuity is typically in the 20/50 to 20/200 range. Answer "A" refers to the congenital color blindness entities (e.g. protanopia). Patients with these disorders have normal visual acuity and lack of retinal findings. Answer "B" refers to the cone dystrophies which can also present with a Bulls eye maculopathy. However, the end visual acuity is much worse compared to Stargardt patients. In addition, Stargardt itself does not confer any color vision defects. "Hemeralopia" (i.e. day-blindness) occurs in patients with cone dystrophies whereby their vision is actually worse in bright light conditions. Answer "C" refers to the peculiar FA phenomenon that can occur in birdshot chorioretinopathy (one of the white-dot syndromes).

question: Which of the following newborns should be screened for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) (assume that all newborns have a stable clinical course)?

options.A: born with birth weight of 2000 grams or less
options.B: born with birth weight of 2500 grams or less
options.C: born at gestational age of 30 weeks or earlier
options.D: born at gestational age of 32 weeks or earlier

explanation: Premature infants should undergo a dilated fundus exam (DFE) to screen for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) if they were born at gestational age of 30 weeks or earlier or had a birth weight of 1500 grams or less. Screening for ROP should also occur in premature infants with an unstable course if the pediatrician feels that the child is at high risk for ROP. Some guidelines for ROP screening: Perform first DFE at 4 weeks' chronologic age, or at corrected gestational age of 30-31 weeks, whichever is later (but no later than 6 weeks' chronologic age). In other words, the more pre-term an infant is at birth, the longer the time to develop serious ROP. Thus, by starting the screening later, you will minimize the number of traumatic eye exams while not missing the developing of serious ROP. For example, if an infant is born at 30 weeks gestational age, you would not screen her until she was 34 weeks gestational age (i.e. 4 weeks' chronologic age). Cyclomydril (0.2% cyclopentolate and 1.0% phenylephrine) is recommended for DFE for these infants. The infant may experience apnea & bradycardia during the DFE and thus the NICU nurse should be present during the exam. The ETROP (Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity) classification of ROP: o Type 1 ROP § Zone I, any stage, with plus disease § Zone I, stage 3 without plus disease § Zone II, stage 2 or 3 with plus disease o Type 2 ROP § Zone I, stage 1 or 2 without plus disease § Zone II, stage 3 without plus disease Treatment (i.e. scatter laser to the peripheral avascular retina) is done for Type I ROP; close observation is done for Type II ROP.

question: A 3-year-old patient with an uncomplicated prenatal and postnatal history presents to your clinic with unilateral leukocoria of the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrates a funnel-shaped retinal detachment, normal axial length, and no discrete masses or calcification. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The differential diagnosis for leukocoria is high-yield for board exams. It is the most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma in the United States and other developed countries, but can be caused by many other disease entities. A differential diagnosis for leukocoria is shown below. Tumors: retinoblastoma, medulloepithelioma, leukemia, astrocytic hamartoma (retinal astrocytoma), combined retinal hamartoma Congenital: persistent fetal vasculature, posterior coloboma, Norrie’s disease, incontinentia pigmenti, retinal dysplasia, cataract Vascular disease: retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), Coat’s disease, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy Trauma: vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment Inflammatory: toxocariasis, toxoplasmosis, endophthalmitis, posterior uveitis Fluorescein angiography demonstrates vascular nonperfusion in the eye without leukocoria representing bilateral disease. In the absence of premature birth (< 30 weeks’ gestational age), low birthweight (< 1500 g), excessive supplemental oxygen, or poor postnatal growth, retinopathy of prematurity is less likely and this presentation is more consistent with familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR). FEVR is a primarily autosomal dominant disease where there is incomplete vascularization of the peripheral retina to vascularize. Fundus exam will typically show avascularity of the temporal retina with varying degrees of fibrovascular proliferation that can mimic ROP. FEVR is bilateral but can be highly asymmetric. In this case, the patient has a complete funnel retinal detachment in the right eye and only mild avascularity in the left eye. Management options depend on the clinical stage of the disease but can include photocoagulation, cryopexy, vitrectomy, cataract extraction, and anti-VEGF injections. OPTIC DISC ABNORMALITIES.

explanation: The disc photos demonstrate temporal pallor with an area of "triangular excavation." In addition, there is an absence of fine superficial capillaries of the temporal aspect of the disc. This young girl also displays slow loss of vision and absence of nystagmus. These features are characteristic of dominant optic atrophy which is also known as Kjer optic atrophy. Other features of dominant optic atrophy are: autosomal dominant inheritance, blue-yellow (i.e. tritan) dyschromatopsia, mild-to-moderate vision loss (20/40-20/200) level, and overall acceptable prognosis (i.e. vision rarely worse than 20/200). It is the most common of the hereditary optic atrophies and is associated with mutations in the OPA1 gene. In contrast, there exists an autosomal recessive optic atrophy that begins earlier in childhood (e.g. prior to 5 years of age) with much more severe vision loss and also nystagmus in ~50% of cases. (Answer choices "A" and "C"). Answer choice "B" refers to the mitochondrial inheritance of Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, which therefore can only be passed along by females. It usually affects males in their second or third decade of life. Behr optic atrophy is another hereditary optic atrophy which is much rarer than the above diseases. Its clinical features are: onset of vision loss in early childhood (i.e. <10 years old), ataxia, intellectual disability, and urinary incontinence. question: The retinal finding in the photograph above along the superotemporal arcade is found on a routine eye exam in a 7-year-old patient who appears otherwise healthy. What is an additional concern in any child with this finding?
explanation: The photograph above shows a large white feathery lesion following the superotemporal arcade that appears classic for a myelinated nerve fiber layer. Myelinated nerve fiber layer (NFL) lesions are present from early in life and represent a focal abnormality in normal myelination. Myelination of retinal ganglion cells generally starts at the lateral geniculate ganglion and stops at the lamina cribrosa, although for unknown reason myelination extends into the retinal nerve fiber layer in some patients. Lesions can be large or small, generally follow a vascular distribution, frequently appear adjacent to the optic nerve head (less apparent in this case), and can result in a relative scotoma corresponding to the region of aberrant myelination. Myelinated NFL is one cause of pseudopapilledema when the area of myelination occurs circumferentially around the optic nerve head. For unclear reasons, children with myelinated nerve fiber layers are at increased risk for refractive amblyopia and should undergo careful visual acuity testing and refraction since correction of the refractive error may reverse the vision loss. HIV (or more appropriately AIDS) can make patients susceptible to cytomegalovirus retinitis which can show white exudates in the retina but there is usually hemorrhage, retinal necrosis / swelling, and the patient with a lesion this size should be symptomatic. Cotton wool spots (CWS) are white retinal lesions caused by infarcts in the NFL often associated with hypertension but CWS are usually smaller and this patient shows no other findings of HTN such as hemorrhages, microaneurysms, or arterial vascular changes.

question: Which of the following causes of decreased vision from birth would demonstrate an abnormal fundus appearance if checked within the first few months of life?
explanation: De Morsier syndrome, or septo-optic dysplasia (SOD), is a congenital disease marked by midline brain developmental abnormalities and unilateral or bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia. Vision can range from near normal to severely impaired. Nystagmus is frequently present and develops around age 1-4 months when the pathways required for normal fixation typically mature. In children with SOD, the diagnosis is not typically a mystery because the fundus exam will show optic nerve hypoplasia from birth (although it may be difficult for the novice to see in a screaming child with nystagmus). Achromatopsia, or rod monochromatism, is an autosomal recessive condition marked by congenital absence of cone cells leading to poor central vision, no color vision, and nystagmus. The retinal exam is usually normal. Leber's congenital amaurosis (LCA) is an autosomal recessive disorder of rods and cones that can be thought of as a severe form of retinitis pigmentosa. Vision is usually poor and pupillary responses are sluggish. The retinal exam can vary widely but is usually normal early in life and becomes similar to retinitis pigmentosa over time (bone spicules, optic nerve pallor, attenuated vessels, etc). Both LCA and achromatopsia may require an ERG for diagnosis early in life and are some of the more common causes for abnormal vision with a normal fundus exam in an infant. Cortical visual impairment (CVI) is poor vision due to pathology occurring in the visual pathways somewhere from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. There are many different causes including periventricular leukomalacia, stroke, CNS malformations, and in utero infections. If cortical impairment occurs before the first week or two of life, there may be optic nerve pallor from transynaptic degeneration of retinal ganglion cells although usually CVI patients have normal appearing fundi and ERGs.
